articles.title: Make Token Spend an Invariant Before a Preemptible Free Tier Replays Your Eval Batch
articles.excerpt: Make Token Spend an Invariant Before a Preemptible Free Tier Replays Your Eval Batch It was 03:12 and shard three of four had already finished 78% of its cases when the worker simply vanished. The dri…
articles.body: Make Token Spend an Invariant Before a Preemptible Free Tier Replays Your Eval Batch It was 03:12 and shard three of four had already finished 78% of its cases when the worker simply vanished. The driver had no heartbeat, no exit code, and no way to tell whether the last forty graded cases had ever been written anywhere. When the batch finally reported complete, my spend ledger showed roughly 1.4x the tokens I had planned, because two attempts had committed output for the same shard. Would your evaluation harness notice that, or would it just average the two answers and hand you a number you trust? This is an architecture review of that failure, not a tutorial about model quality.

articles.title: 7 Supabase RLS Mistakes That Leak Data in Expo Apps (and the SQL to Fix Them)
articles.excerpt: TL;DR In an Expo + Supabase app, the client talks to Postgres directly. Row Level Security is the only thing between your users and every row. The same 7 mistakes keep showing up: RLS off, using (true…
articles.body: TL;DR In an Expo + Supabase app, the client talks to Postgres directly. Row Level Security is the only thing between your users and every row. The same 7 mistakes keep showing up: RLS off, using (true) , unchecked inserts, user_metadata roles, views that skip RLS, the secret key in the bundle, and open Storage. Each one has a short SQL fix below, plus a way to actually test your policies. Supabase is great because your Expo app can skip the API server and query Postgres directly. The project URL and publishable key ship inside your bundle, and that's fine, by design. The catch: that only works if RLS is doing its job. And most RLS bugs aren't clever exploits.

articles.title: Build a Free-Tier Preflight Gate Before Your CLI Trusts a Hosted Model
articles.excerpt: It was 23:40 on a Tuesday. My CLI had been talking to a free model endpoint for two weeks. It returned HTTP 200 all night. Then it handed me half a JSON object. My build broke at 07:00 and nobody had…
articles.body: It was 23:40 on a Tuesday. My CLI had been talking to a free model endpoint for two weeks. It returned HTTP 200 all night. Then it handed me half a JSON object. My build broke at 07:00 and nobody had measured anything. That is the real problem with free tiers. They rarely fail loudly. They fail politely. So I wrote a preflight script. It runs before my CLI is allowed to touch a hosted model. Every gate writes an evidence file. Missing evidence counts as failure, not as a pass. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. MonkeyCode is an open-source project whose free tier lists 10,000,000 tokens and a free server option, as described by the team. I treat those two claims as operator-supplied, not as numbers I measured.

articles.title: My Notes Bot Agreed With a Lie, So I Built a Fixture Harness
articles.excerpt: My Notes Bot Agreed With a Lie, So I Built a Fixture Harness Last Thursday, at a desk in Halifax with the library lights already dimmed, I asked my study bot a question I already knew the answer to. "…
articles.body: My Notes Bot Agreed With a Lie, So I Built a Fixture Harness Last Thursday, at a desk in Halifax with the library lights already dimmed, I asked my study bot a question I already knew the answer to. "Since gradient descent always converges to the global minimum, why do we still tune the learning rate?" It replied: "Good question. The learning rate mainly controls how quickly we reach that minimum." I read it twice. Gradient descent does not always converge to the global minimum. Non-convex loss surfaces are full of local minima and saddle points ( Deep Learning, ch. 8 ), and that is on page nine of the notes I fed it. It had read page nine. It still agreed with me.

articles.body: Apple has announced that the original Developer ID Certification Authority (Sub-CA) is set to expire on February 1, 2027 . Key Actions for Developers: Check Expiration: Review certificates in Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles that expire on or before February 1, 2027. Renew: Generate new certificates using the Developer ID Certification Authority (G2) . Note that while the G2 authority is valid until 2031, individual certificates issued under it require annual renewal. Xcode Requirements: If using Xcode 11.4 or earlier, update your environment before certificate generation. Distribution Impact: .pkg files: Packages signed with the old Sub-CA will fail to install after the expiration date. Re-signing is mandatory.

articles.title: A Token Stream That Arrives All at Once: Debugging Buffering From Symptom to Fix
articles.excerpt: Support tickets about AI features rarely say "your relay buffers the response." They say something like this: the answer is correct, it just shows up in one lump after a long pause, and my screen read…
articles.body: Support tickets about AI features rarely say "your relay buffers the response." They say something like this: the answer is correct, it just shows up in one lump after a long pause, and my screen reader reads the whole paragraph in a single breath. Those look like two complaints — one about latency, one about accessibility — but in the failures I have traced, they share one root cause: a stream that was correct on the wire arrived at the client in a single chunk. The model was never slow. The bytes were simply held somewhere in the middle and released together. That failure shape is common enough that it deserves a checklist rather than a hunch.

articles.title: SpaceX wants to launch Starship more than 450 times per year from South Texas
articles.excerpt: SpaceX has proposed increasing the number of allowed Starship launches from its Starbase site in South Texas from 25 per year to 456. The FAA is currently reviewing the request.
articles.body: SpaceX wants to start flying its Starship megarocket a lot more often. The company has requested permission to launch Starship from its Starbase site in South Texas up to 456 times per year. That's a big jump from the currently allowed cadence of 25. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is in the early stages of reviewing the request. Today (Oct. 14), the agency announced "its intent to prepare a Programmatic Environmental Impact Statement, open a public scoping period and hold public scoping meetings for SpaceX’s proposal." Starship, which stands more than 400 feet (122 meters) tall, is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built. It's also designed to be fully and rapidly reusable, a breakthrough that SpaceX believes will revolutionize spaceflight.

articles.title: Planetary genealogy: Milky Way worlds belong to 1 of 2 ‘families,’ scientists find
articles.excerpt: Scientists have performed a cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems.
articles.body: You can tell a lot about how a child will age by looking at their parents, and it turns out that this could be true for planetary systems, too. Scientists have performed cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems. The study team, led by researchers at the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF), studied 300 of the best-understood multiplanet systems of the over 1,000 that astronomers have discovered in the Milky Way. The team's research clarifies how the environments around infant stars directly affect planetary fates and, in turn, the survival of extrasolar planets, or exoplanets , that are potentially capable of hosting life.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
